STRUCTURAL PEST CONTROL INSPECTION REPORT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 · Pat Morgan

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's structural pest control inspection report requirements (Business and Professions Code §§ 8516-8519, and the related delivery requirement in Civil Code § 1099) as they may apply to the property at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, as between Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee. It states what California law provides on this subject. It does not authorize, direct, or prepare any inspection report, certification, or notice, and it does not resolve whether an inspection report or certification is a condition of any specific contract or financing arrangement.

WHEN A STRUCTURAL PEST CONTROL INSPECTION REPORT MUST BE DELIVERED TO A BUYER
Separately from Business and Professions Code §§ 8516-8519 (which govern how a structural pest control inspection report and certification must be prepared once one exists), California's Civil Code states a distinct delivery-to-buyer rule keyed to whether the report was called for in the first place. As soon as practical before transfer of title of real property (or execution of a real property sales contract), a transferor or the transferor's agent must deliver to the transferee a copy of a structural pest control inspection report, upon which a certification may be made, provided that certification or preparation of a report is a condition of the contract effecting the transfer, or is a requirement imposed as a condition of financing the transfer. If a notice of work completed, or a certification, is received by the transferor or the transferor's agent before transfer of title, it must likewise be furnished to the transferee as soon as practical before transfer of title. Noncompliance does not by itself invalidate the transfer, unless the noncompliance is separately a valid ground for rescission.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "As soon as practical before transfer of title of any real property or the execution of a real property sales contract as defined in Section 2985, the transferor, fee owner, or his or her agent, shall deliver to the transferee a copy of a structural pest control inspection report prepared pursuant to Section 8516 of the Business and Professions Code upon which any certification in accordance with Section 8519 of the Business and Professions Code may be made, provided that certification or preparation of a report is a condition of the contract effecting that transfer, or is a requirement imposed as a condition of financing such transfer."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1099(a), California Civil Code, delivery of a structural pest control inspection report conditioned on it being a contract or financing condition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1099.)
  "No transfer of title of real property shall be invalidated solely because of the failure of any person to comply with the provisions of this section unless such failure is an act or omission which would be a valid ground for rescission of such transfer in the absence of this section."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1099(d), California Civil Code, noncompliance doesn't by itself invalidate the transfer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1099.)
  Known gap: This statute's delivery duty is conditional, not universal: its own text ties the duty to certification or preparation of a report being a condition of the contract effecting the transfer, or a requirement imposed as a condition of financing the transfer -- this document does not determine, for any specific transaction, whether a report or certification is in fact such a condition (for example, because a purchase contract requires one, or because a lender requires one for the loan). Where no report or certification is a condition of the contract or of financing, this specific delivery duty, by its own terms, does not apply -- this document takes no position on whether some other disclosure duty might separately require disclosing a known infestation. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction structures a report-delivery duty tied to a real estate transfer -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transaction. The two citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Civil Code § 1099) rather than independently authored sources.

WHO MUST PERFORM THE INSPECTION, AND WHEN THE REPORT MUST BE DELIVERED
California's Structural Pest Control Act, within the Business and Professions Code, applies these requirements only to "wood destroying pests or organisms." A registered structural pest control company or licensee may not commence work on a contract, or sign, issue, or deliver any document expressing an opinion or statement about the absence or presence of wood destroying pests or organisms, until an inspection has been made by a licensed Branch 3 field representative or operator employed by a registered company (subject to a narrow statutory exception). A written inspection report conforming to the statute, on a board-approved form, must then be prepared and delivered to the person who requested the inspection and to the property owner (or the owner's designated agent) within 10 business days from the start of the inspection -- except that a report prepared for use by an attorney for litigation purposes need not be delivered to the board or the property owner. The report must be delivered before work is commenced on the property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A registered company or licensee shall not commence work on a contract, or sign, issue, or deliver any documents expressing an opinion or statement relating to the absence or presence of wood destroying pests or organisms until an inspection has been made by a licensed Branch 3 field representative or operator employed by a registered company, except as provided in Section 8519.5."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 8516(b), California Business and Professions Code, inspection must be made by a licensed Branch 3 field representative or operator of a registered company (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=8516.)
  "A written inspection report conforming to this section and a form approved by the board shall be prepared and delivered to the person requesting the inspection and the property owner, or to the property owner’s designated agent, within 10 business days from the start of the inspection, except that an inspection report prepared for use by an attorney for litigation purposes is not required to be reported to the board or the property owner."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 8516(b) [report delivery timing], California Business and Professions Code, written report must be delivered within 10 business days (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=8516.)
  Known gap: This clause states only what Business and Professions Code § 8516(b) itself requires once an inspection and report are undertaken; it does not state whether a specific transaction requires an inspection to be ordered in the first place (see the separate clause on the Civil Code § 1099 delivery trigger), nor does it list every item the statute requires the report itself to contain (subdivision (b) goes on to list thirteen specific content requirements, including a foundation diagram, roof-inspection statement, and a mandatory notice about the right to a second opinion, which are not quoted here). This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction licenses and times a structural pest inspection report -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transaction. The two citations below are both from subdivision (b) of the same statutory section (Business and Professions Code § 8516) rather than independently authored sources. Business and Professions Code § 8520, sometimes assumed to be part of this inspection-report framework, is not: it is a separate, independent section (opening a different article of the same chapter) that establishes the existence of the Structural Pest Control Board and is subject to its own sunset/repeal date, and it is not cited here as authority for any inspection-report requirement.

THE REPORT'S DISTINCTION BETWEEN EVIDENT INFESTATION AND CONDITIONS LIKELY TO LEAD TO INFESTATION
California's structural pest control inspection statute distinguishes, in its own text, between two categories of finding. On request at the time a report is ordered, a registered company or licensee must separately identify, for each recommendation for corrective measures: (1) the infestation or infection that is evident, and (2) the conditions that are present that are deemed likely to lead to infestation or infection. The board-prescribed inspection report form itself is required to separately identify these same two categories. The statute states that, in no event may a condition deemed likely to lead to infestation or infection be characterized as an actual "defect" or an actual "active" infestation or infection, or as needing correction as a precondition to issuing a certification.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(1) The infestation or infection that is evident. (2) The conditions that are present that are deemed likely to lead to infestation or infection."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 8516(c), California Business and Professions Code, the two categories a requested separate report must identify (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=8516.)
  "In no event, however, shall conditions deemed likely to lead to infestation or infection be characterized as actual “defects” or as actual “active” infestations or infections or in need of correction as a precondition to issuing a certification pursuant to Section 8519."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 8516(e), California Business and Professions Code, a likely-to-lead condition may not be characterized as an actual defect or active infestation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=8516.)
  Known gap: This clause states the statute's own two-category distinction; it does not itself label these categories as "Section 1" and "Section 2" (a naming convention used on the board-prescribed inspection report form and in general industry usage) -- that form's exact current wording could not be independently verified from a fetchable primary source within this research, so this clause states the statutory text underlying the distinction rather than the form's own labels. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction's inspection-report statute distinguishes evident infestation from conditions likely to lead to infestation -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transaction or property. The two citations below are both from Business and Professions Code § 8516, one from subdivision (c) and one from subdivision (e) of that same section, rather than independently authored sources.

THE OPTIONAL CERTIFICATION OF NO ACTIVE INFESTATION
Separately from the inspection report itself, California law provides for an optional "certification." A registered company that makes an inspection report must, if requested by the person who ordered the report, prepare and deliver to that person (or a designated agent) a certification. Where the inspection report disclosed no infestation or infection, the statute specifies the certification's text: "This is to certify that the above property was inspected on ____ (date(s)) in accordance with the Structural Pest Control Act and rules and regulations adopted pursuant thereto, and that no evidence of active infestation or infection was found in the visible and accessible areas." The statute specifies different required text for a certification issued after disclosed infestation or infection has been corrected, or corrected only in part, and for a certification following a limited inspection report.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Any registered company which makes an inspection report pursuant to Section 8516, shall, if requested by the person ordering the inspection report, prepare and deliver to that person or his or her designated agent, a certification, to provide:"
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 8519, California Business and Professions Code, certification must be prepared and delivered if requested (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=8519.)
  "This is to certify that the above property was inspected on ____ (date(s)) in accordance with the Structural Pest Control Act and rules and regulations adopted pursuant thereto, and that no evidence of active infestation or infection was found in the visible and accessible areas."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 8519(a), California Business and Professions Code, statutory certification text where no infestation or infection was disclosed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=8519.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the certification text for the "no infestation disclosed" scenario; the statute specifies three additional certification texts (for completed correction, partial correction, and a limited-inspection-report scenario) that are not separately quoted here. Certification is requested, not automatic -- this clause does not state that a certification is issued in every transaction where an inspection report exists. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction structures a post-inspection certification -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transaction. The two citations below are both from Business and Professions Code § 8519 rather than independently authored sources.

LATER CORRESPONDENCE MUST REFERENCE THE REPORT, AND COMPLETED WORK MUST BE NOTICED
California law extends the inspection-report requirement to later documents. Any work contract, billing, agreement, letter of work completed, or other correspondence or document expressing an opinion or making a statement about the presence or absence of wood destroying pests or organisms must refer to the inspection report, and must specifically indicate whether all of the report's recommended work was completed or, if not, which recommendations were not completed. Separately, when a registered company completes work under a contract, it must prepare, on a board-prescribed form, a notice of work completed and not completed, and furnish that notice to the property owner (or the owner's agent) within 10 business days after completing the work; the notice must state the cost of the completed work and the estimated cost of work not completed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Any work contract, billing, agreement, letter of work completed, or other correspondence or document expressing an opinion or making a statement relating to the presence or absence of wood destroying pests or organisms, shall refer to the inspection report required by Section 8516. These documents shall indicate specifically whether all of the recommended work as set forth in the inspection report was completed, or, if not, the document shall indicate specifically which recommendations were not completed."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 8517, California Business and Professions Code, later documents must refer to the inspection report and completion status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=8517.)
  "When a registered company completes work under a contract, it shall prepare, on a form prescribed by the board, a notice of work completed and not completed, and shall furnish that notice to the owner of the property or the owner’s agent within 10 business days after completing the work. The notice shall include a statement of the cost of the completed work and estimated cost of work not completed."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 8518(a), California Business and Professions Code, notice of work completed and not completed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=8518.)
  Known gap: This clause does not state whether any particular correspondence or billing document falls within the described category, or whether any particular work has in fact been completed. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction ties later correspondence and work-completion notices back to the original inspection report -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transaction. The two citations below are from two separate, independently authored sections of the same statutory chapter (Business and Professions Code §§ 8517 and 8518), not subsections of a single section.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
This information sheet regarding structural pest control inspection reports under California's Business and Professions Code, concerning the property at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 as between Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee, states California law as of the date below. It does not constitute legal advice about, and does not resolve, any specific inspection, infestation, or disclosure question.
